description: We are a team of 6 working on the "Dancing with the SARs
summary: Stillwater turns NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar images into a field-survey tool for the Mekong Delta flood season. Monsoon clouds blank out optical satellites: across the 2026 season only 2 of 51 optical passes over Thạnh Mỹ Tây were usable (0 of 54 over the Giồng Riềng cluster), while NISAR saw the ground on all 11 passes (17 Jun–27 Oct 2026). Stillwater reads each 10 m pixel's HV backscatter, finds pixels that stay smooth (a "water signal") for 24, 36, 48 or 60+ days, groups them into 500 m cells and cross-checks them against OPERA DSWx-S1 surface water. Planners of flood-season livelihood projects, such as rice–fish farming, get an interactive map, a bilingual Vietnamese–English story page and a CSV survey list showing where to look first: 12,395 ha in Thạnh Mỹ Tây and 16,621 ha in the Giồng Riềng cluster show a continuous water signal for 48+ days. It is a screening tool, not a validated flood map; field validation is the next step.
details:
The problem we started from

In the flood season, planners at agricultural extension services and NGOs such as WWF's Mekong programme have to decide which fields to survey for rice–fish pilots. The delta is flat and cut up by dikes and canals, so a river gauge tells you the level of the river and very little about the field behind the dike. Nobody can walk tens of thousands of hectares either.

2026 made the question harder. Mekong River Commission data for Châu Đốc show that the flood peaked on 25 September, the earliest of the six years from 2021 to 2026, and the 10–20 October average was 2.38 m, which is 0.46 m below the 2021–2025 average.

Optical satellites do not help much in the monsoon. We measured cloud on the exact frames we analyse, using the Fmask layer that comes with NASA's HLS product (Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9). Between 17 June and 27 October there were 51 optical acquisitions over Thạnh Mỹ Tây and only 2 were usable, which for us means less than 20% cloud, cloud shadow or cloud edge and at least 90% of the frame covered. Over the four-commune Giồng Riềng cluster there were 54 acquisitions and none were usable. NISAR's radar saw the ground on all 11 of its passes.

Figure 1. The same frame over Thạnh Mỹ Tây. Left: Sentinel-2, 6 September, about 62% cloud and shadow. Right: NISAR L-band, 9 September.

What Stillwater does

Stillwater turns the NISAR time series into something a planner can use without reading radar. It has three parts.

  • A map. For each of four areas you can see where the ground showed a water signal for at least 24, 36, 48 or 60 days in a row. Clicking a 500 m cell opens its history across the 11 passes.
  • Checks against a second satellite. One mode puts NISAR next to OPERA surface water, and a two-date tab shows what changed between any two passes.
  • A survey list. Cells can be added with a note, printed, or exported as a CSV with coordinates so a field team can take it along.

There is also a story page in Vietnamese and English that walks through the same data for people who have never looked at a radar image. Both the story page and the map are static web pages, so they load quickly on a poor connection.

Figure 2. The Stillwater dashboard for Thạnh Mỹ Tây. Blue marks ground that showed a water signal for at least 48 days in a row.

How it works

We used NISAR L2 GCOV files from the ASF archive: 11 acquisitions on track 47 (frames 83 and 84) between 17 June and 27 October 2026, one every 12 days. The 4 August pass is missing. The data are 10 m pixels with HH and HV backscatter. For each date and area we cut out the frame, smoothed the HV power with a 3×3 window and converted it to dB.

A smooth, open water surface sends very little energy back in cross-polarisation, so flooded ground looks dark in HV. We call a pixel a water signal when HV is below −23 dB. We did not pick that number out of the air. OPERA water pixels in our frames have a median HV of about −24 to −25 dB, and a −24 dB threshold caught only 33–78% of them, while −23 dB gave the best balance across areas and dates. We have to be upfront that we chose it after looking at OPERA, so the agreement figures further down are somewhat optimistic.

One dark pixel on one date is not enough. A field that was just harvested or levelled is also smooth. So Stillwater only counts runs of at least three consecutive passes, which is 24 days or more, and reports how long the longest run was. The results are rolled up into 500 m cells, which is a unit a field team can actually go and look at.

Two details cost us some time. The last scene (27 October) comes from a newer processing version of the product (P05036, while the other ten are P05023) and sits about 0.5 dB lower than the others on stable bright targets such as buildings, in all four frames. We added 0.5 dB to that date before thresholding. Without it Giồng Riềng appeared to jump on the last date, which would have been an artefact. The second detail is Tràm Chim National Park, which covers 244 of the 1,225 cells in our Tràm Chim reference frame (boundary from OpenStreetMap relation 7146562). Water in the park is managed for conservation, so we kept those cells out of the rankings.

What we found

In Thạnh Mỹ Tây the share of the frame with a water signal went from 14% on 16 August to 50% on 28 August, peaked at 58% on 21 September and was down to 37% by 27 October. 12,395 ha of the 39,223 ha frame (32%) had a signal for at least 48 days in a row.

Giồng Riềng behaves differently. The share rose from 16% in mid-August to 31% on 28 August and 9 September, reached 46% on 21 September and kept climbing to 53–54% in October. It had not turned down by 27 October, while the river at Châu Đốc was already falling. That gauge is about 95 km away, so we deliberately do not draw it next to Giồng Riềng. 16,621 ha of the 55,863 ha frame had a signal for at least 48 days.

Figure 3. Thạnh Mỹ Tây on four NISAR passes. Blue is the water signal (HV below −23 dB).

Figure 4. Share of each frame with a water signal on every NISAR pass. The two areas peak at different times.

Checking the result against OPERA

NISAR is L-band. OPERA DSWx-S1 is a 30 m surface-water product made from Sentinel-1, which is C-band, so it is a different satellite with a different wavelength and a useful second opinion. In Thạnh Mỹ Tây, 82–87% of the 500 m cells that stayed dark from 28 August through 15 October are mostly water on 17 October according to OPERA. Cells that were dark on 28 August and bright again by 15 October are only 0–4% water by OPERA (4% in Thạnh Mỹ Tây, 0% in the Tràm Chim reference frame). That fits bare or freshly worked fields rather than standing water, and it is the reason for the three-pass rule.

For Giồng Riềng the OPERA overpasses are about four days away from ours, so we only claim that the trend agrees. Among pixels with a water signal for 48 days or more, 47% are water in OPERA on 10–11 October and 76% on 22–23 October, which is what you would expect if the water there was still rising.

Figure 5. OPERA comparison mode: NISAR water signal in blue on the left, OPERA water in green on the right, with a slider in between.

What it does not tell you

A water signal is a smooth surface. That is usually water but it can also be a bare or levelled field, and OPERA is radar too, so the two agreeing is not the same as a field measurement. We have not been to these fields yet. A 500 m cell can also be half flooded and half dry, so the cell list is for finding places to go, and the pixel layer on the map is where the actual boundary is. NISAR comes back every 12 days and the files take time to reach the archive, so this cannot warn anyone about a flood by the hour. It is for reviewing a season. And NISAR only launched in 2025, so there is no earlier NISAR flood season to compare with. For the 2021–2025 background we used the river gauge record instead.

What comes next

The first job is field checks. We want to take the top cells in Thạnh Mỹ Tây out with extension staff, see whether there is water, and count how many of the list hold up. That share is how we would judge whether Stillwater is useful. After that we want to rerun the pipeline after each NISAR pass in the 2027 season instead of at the end, bring in the HH channel to tell rice standing in water from open water, and add new areas, which only needs a bounding box and the matching files.

Built with

Python (NumPy, rasterio, h5py, pyproj) for the NISAR, OPERA and HLS processing. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web app, MapLibre GL JS for the dashboard map and Three.js for the field cross-section on the story page. Hosting is on Cloudflare Pages.
